reigns.tagline: The pagan duke who signed Poland up to Christendom
reigns.previously: Pagan tribes on the Warta, squeezed between Germans and Czechs.
paragraphs: Around 960 the Polans were a pagan people living in forts of earth and timber along the Warta. To the west were the Saxon lords of the German Empire, hungry for land and converts. To the south sat Christian Bohemia. Their duke was Mieszko, and the first time anyone writes his name down, in a Saxon chronicle of the 960s, he is already fighting. He had warriors, silver and a problem: pagans made easy targets.

His answer was a marriage. In 965 he wed Dobrawa, a Czech princess, and in 966 he was baptised. That date is still counted as the birth of Poland. Christianity put him on the map as a ruler the emperor had to deal with. In 972 he smashed the German margrave Hodo at Cedynia. Near the end of his life he placed his lands under the pope's protection in a document known by its odd opening words, "Dagome iudex".
He died in May 992. The document named his second wife Oda and her sons, which suggests he meant to share the realm among his heirs.

claims.text: Dobrawa talked Mieszko into becoming a Christian.
claims.note: Thietmar of Merseburg, writing about 50 years later, credits her, and Gallus repeats it. It makes a neat story, but the deal clearly suited Mieszko's politics too.

claims.text: Mieszko beat Margrave Hodo at Cedynia in 972.
claims.note: Thietmar records the battle; his own father fought on the losing side.

claims.text: The "Dagome iudex" puts Mieszko's lands under the protection of the pope.
claims.note: Only an 11th-century summary survives, and the garbled names ("Dagome") are still argued over, but the gist is accepted.

reigns.hook: Mieszko is dead and his lands are meant to be shared. His eldest son, Bolesław, has other ideas. His stepmother and half-brothers are about to find out.

reigns.tagline: The warrior who made his father's duchy a kingdom
reigns.previously: Mieszko I dies in 992, leaving his lands to be shared among his sons.
paragraphs: Poles call him Chrobry, "the Brave". He began by throwing his stepmother Oda and her sons out of the country, then spent 30 years fighting almost everyone nearby. When the missionary bishop Adalbert of Prague was killed by pagan Prussians in 997, Bolesław paid for the body and enshrined it at Gniezno. Within two years Adalbert was a saint, and pilgrims were coming.

In 1000 the young Emperor Otto III came on pilgrimage to Adalbert's tomb. At the Congress of Gniezno he treated Bolesław as a friend and partner, and Poland got its own archbishop at Gniezno, free of German churchmen. Bolesław then fought Otto's successor Henry II on and off for 15 years and kept most of what he grabbed. In 1018 he marched to Kiev and put his son-in-law on its throne.
His dream was a crown. When Henry II died, Bolesław had himself crowned King of Poland in 1025. He enjoyed it for a few weeks and died in June.

claims.text: Bolesław bought St Adalbert's body from the Prussians for its weight in gold.
claims.note: Gallus Anonymus tells it about a century later. That a ransom was paid is likely; the scales are storytelling.

claims.text: Otto III took his own crown off and set it on Bolesław's head at Gniezno.
claims.note: Gallus says so, but writers closer to the event, like Thietmar, don't. Historians argue over what the gesture meant, if it happened.

claims.text: Bolesław notched his sword on Kiev's Golden Gate, giving Poland's coronation sword Szczerbiec its name.
claims.note: The Golden Gate was built after his raid, and the Szczerbiec now in Wawel dates from the 12th or 13th century.

reigns.hook: The first king of Poland is dead. His son Mieszko is crowned straight away, but two brothers think the crown should have been theirs, and the emperor is listening.

reigns.tagline: The second king, who lost the crown and much more
reigns.cameToPower: Succeeded his father and was crowned
reigns.reignEnded: Died as the realm fell apart
reigns.previously: Bolesław the Brave is crowned king in 1025 and dies weeks later.
paragraphs: Mieszko II was a cultured man. A German duchess, Matilda of Swabia, praised him for praising God in Latin and Greek, and sent him a prayer book with a picture of herself handing it over. His wife Richeza was the late Emperor Otto III's niece. He was crowned king in 1025, and from then on things went downhill.

His wars against Emperor Conrad II went badly. In 1031 the Germans attacked from the west and the Rus from the east at the same time. His elder half-brother Bezprym seized power and sent the crown and regalia to the emperor. Mieszko fled to Bohemia, where the duke threw him in prison. Bezprym was murdered within a year, and Mieszko came back, but only as a duke under the emperor, sharing the land with relatives.
He pulled the country back together by 1033, then died in May 1034. Revolt and chaos followed almost at once.

claims.text: The Bohemians castrated Mieszko while he was their prisoner.
claims.note: Gallus Anonymus says the Czechs mutilated him so he could not father children. Since Casimir was already born, it changed nothing, and no other source confirms it.

claims.text: Bezprym sent the Polish crown and regalia to Emperor Conrad II.
claims.note: Recorded by Conrad's biographer Wipo, writing in the 1040s.

claims.text: Mieszko was murdered.
claims.note: Some historians read hints of a nobles' plot in the thin sources. Most records just note his death.

reigns.hook: Mieszko is dead and Poland comes apart. Nobles turn on his widow, peasants turn on the priests, and his young son Casimir is chased out of the country.

reigns.tagline: The exile who came home to rebuild a ruined country
reigns.reignEnded: Died in his bed at Poznań
reigns.previously: Mieszko II dies in 1034 with Poland falling to pieces.
paragraphs: Casimir inherited a disaster. Within a few years he and his mother were driven out, and Poland collapsed into revolt. Nobles fought each other, and peasants rose against their lords and the new Christian priests. Then Duke Bretislaus of Bohemia rode in, sacked Gniezno and carried off St Adalbert's bones as loot.

Casimir came back in 1039 with German troops and the backing of the emperor. Gniezno was in ruins, so he based himself in Kraków, which became the heart of the kingdom for the next 500 years. He married a sister of the Prince of Kiev, which won him Rus help to beat a rival who had set up his own state in Masovia. He got Silesia back from the Czechs, though he had to pay for it.
He never wore a crown. When he died in 1058, Poland was whole again, and it passed to his eldest son, Bolesław.

claims.text: Casimir spent his exile as a monk at Cluny and needed the pope's permission to leave.
claims.note: The story is told in later Polish chronicles and polished by Długosz. No early record places him at Cluny.

claims.text: Bretislaus of Bohemia carried St Adalbert's relics off to Prague.
claims.note: Cosmas of Prague describes the raid in loving detail. Prague cathedral still claims the bones.

claims.text: A pagan revolt swept Poland in the 1030s.
claims.note: Gallus and later chroniclers describe it. Some historians think its scale and its pagan side have been exaggerated.

reigns.hook: Casimir is dead. His son Bolesław is young, brave and ambitious. He wants the crown his father never wore, and he will not let a bishop stand in his way.

reigns.tagline: The bold king who killed a bishop and lost everything
reigns.previously: Casimir the Restorer dies in 1058, leaving Poland back on its feet.
paragraphs: Bolesław the Bold, also called "the Generous", was a fighter and a showman. He put his own candidates on the thrones of Hungary and Kiev. When the pope and the German emperor went to war over who controlled the Church, Bolesław backed Pope Gregory VII. His reward was a crown: on Christmas Day 1076 he was crowned king at Gniezno.

Then came the scandal that wrecked him. Bishop Stanisław of Kraków quarrelled with the king, and on 11 April 1079 he was killed on Bolesław's orders. Why is still a mystery. Gallus Anonymus, writing a generation later, calls the bishop a traitor. The Church made him a martyr and later a saint, the patron of Poland.
Within months the nobles rose against Bolesław, and he fled with his son to Hungary. He died in exile a couple of years later.

claims.text: Bolesław struck down Bishop Stanisław himself, at the altar, during Mass.
claims.note: This version comes from the bishop's 13th-century saint's life, written for his canonisation. Gallus only says the king had him mutilated as a traitor.

claims.text: Stanisław was a traitor plotting with Bolesław's brother.
claims.note: Gallus hints at it; the Church tradition calls him a martyr for rebuking the king's sins. Historians still argue.

claims.text: Bolesław ended his days as a penitent monk at Ossiach in Carinthia.
claims.note: A late legend, linked to a gravestone there. There's no early evidence he ever reached Austria.

reigns.hook: The king has fled in disgrace. His quiet younger brother takes over, swaps the crown for a duke's title and hands the real power to a man the whole court will learn to hate.

reigns.tagline: The quiet duke whose minister ran the show
reigns.cameToPower: Took over when his brother fled
reigns.previously: Bolesław the Bold flees to Hungary after killing Bishop Stanisław.
paragraphs: Władysław Herman was everything his brother wasn't: cautious, peaceable and happy to be a duke. He never tried for a crown and kept on good terms with the German emperor, whose sister he married. He had two sons by two different women: Zbigniew, the elder, and Bolesław, born in 1086.

The man who really ran Poland was the palatine Sieciech, the duke's chief officer. He built castles, filled offices with his own men, and was widely suspected of wanting the throne. The nobles hated him. Eventually so did both of Władysław's sons, who joined forces, raised troops and forced their father to send Sieciech away around 1100.
Władysław had already split the land between the boys. When he died at Płock in 1102, each brother had his own territory and his own army.

claims.text: Bolesław was born after his parents sent gifts to the monks of Saint-Gilles in Provence to pray for a son.
claims.note: Gallus Anonymus tells the story as a near-miracle. That the gifts were sent is plausible.

claims.text: Sieciech plotted to seize the throne.
claims.note: Gallus says so, but he wrote for Bolesław, who had every reason to blacken the palatine.

claims.text: Władysław never took the title of king.
claims.note: No coronation is recorded, and charters and Gallus call him duke.

reigns.hook: The old duke is dead. Two half-brothers share Poland, and neither trusts the other. Only one of them will keep his eyes.

reigns.tagline: Conqueror, brother-blinder and the man who split Poland
reigns.cameToPower: Shared the realm with his brother
reigns.reignEnded: Died; his will split the realm
reigns.previously: Władysław Herman dies in 1102, leaving Poland split between two sons.
paragraphs: Bolesław Wrymouth (Krzywousty in Polish, perhaps from a crooked jaw) spent his first years fighting his half-brother Zbigniew. By 1107 he had driven him out. In 1109 Emperor Henry V invaded to put Zbigniew back, and was beaten off at the siege of Głogów. Then Bolesław let Zbigniew come home, and in 1112 had him blinded. He died soon after.

The deed horrified people. Bolesław fasted for 40 days and went on pilgrimage to be forgiven. Then he went back to war. Over the next ten years he conquered Pomerania and opened Poland to the Baltic. At his court a foreign monk known as Gallus Anonymus wrote the first history of Poland, starring Bolesław.
Before he died in 1138 he left a will. It split Poland among his sons, with the eldest in Kraków as senior duke over the rest. The aim was peace.

claims.text: At Głogów the Germans tied Polish hostage children to their siege engines, and the defenders kept fighting.
claims.note: Gallus Anonymus tells it; he was writing a few years later for Bolesław. No German source mentions it.

claims.text: Psie Pole, "Dogs' Field" near Wrocław, is named after the dogs that fed on German dead in 1109.
claims.note: The battle first appears in Wincenty Kadłubek, about 90 years later. Gallus, writing only a few years after 1109, never mentions it.

claims.text: Bolesław had Zbigniew blinded and then did public penance.
claims.note: Gallus, who admired Bolesław, records both the blinding and the penance.

reigns.hook: Bolesław's will was meant to keep his sons in harmony. Within eight years the eldest is fighting the others, and Poland breaks apart for nearly two centuries.

reigns.title: The Kingdom in Pieces
reigns.tagline: A will, five brothers and a country torn to shreds
reigns.previously: Bolesław Wrymouth dies, splitting Poland among his sons.
paragraphs: The plan was simple. The eldest Piast would rule from Kraków as senior duke, and the others would obey. It lasted eight years. In 1146 the eldest, Władysław II, was driven out by his half-brothers and died in exile, remembered as "the Exile". Kraków passed to Bolesław IV the Curly, then Mieszko III the Old, then Casimir II the Just, and each branch of the family dug into its own lands.

The duchies grew apart. In 1226 Konrad of Masovia, tired of pagan Prussian raids, invited the Teutonic Knights, German crusading monks, to deal with them. It was a choice Poland would regret for 300 years. The next year Duke Leszek the White was ambushed and murdered at a meeting of princes at Gąsawa.
Then the Mongols came. In 1241 they burned Kraków. On 9 April, at Legnica, they destroyed the army of Duke Henry II the Pious and cut off his head.

claims.text: A trumpeter on Kraków's St Mary's tower was shot in the throat by a Tatar arrow mid-tune, which is why the hourly bugle call stops short.
claims.note: There's no medieval record of it. The story seems to have become popular only in the 20th century.

claims.text: The Mongols paraded Henry the Pious's head on a spear outside Legnica castle.
claims.note: Shown in the Hedwig Codex of 1353 and retold by Długosz a century later. His death in the battle is certain; the details are not.

claims.text: Konrad of Masovia invited the Teutonic Knights into Poland in the 1220s.
claims.note: Documented in the Knights' own records and the emperor's Golden Bull of Rimini.

reigns.hook: Henry the Pious is dead and the Mongols ride away. But the Piast dukes go back to fighting each other, and one day one of them will want to be king again.

reigns.title: Dukes at War
reigns.tagline: Saints, poisoners and a crown nobody can keep
reigns.reignEnded: The Bohemian king is invited in
reigns.previously: The Mongols wipe out Henry the Pious's army at Legnica in 1241.
paragraphs: After Legnica the dukes fought for Kraków again. Bolesław V the Chaste held it for 36 years. His Hungarian wife Kinga was so devout that the couple are said to have lived as brother and sister. She was later made a saint. The Mongols raided again in 1259 and 1287.

Then the ambitious ones moved in. Henry IV Probus, Duke of Wrocław, took Kraków and was plotting a royal crown when he died in 1290. In 1295 Przemysł II of Greater Poland managed it, crowned king at Gniezno, the first in over 200 years. Seven months later he was kidnapped and murdered at Rogoźno.
A tiny, stubborn duke called Władysław tried to take his place and was thrown out. The Polish nobles looked south to the richest king in the region.

claims.text: Kinga threw her ring into a Hungarian salt mine, and it turned up in the first lump of salt dug at Wieliczka.
claims.note: A story from her saint's life. The salt really did make Wieliczka rich, and the mine has a chapel to her.

claims.text: Henry IV Probus was poisoned.
claims.note: Several chroniclers say so, but sudden deaths were often blamed on poison. There's no proof.

claims.text: Przemysł II's murderers worked for the margraves of Brandenburg.
claims.note: Some chroniclers blame Brandenburg, others Polish nobles. Nobody was ever convicted.

reigns.hook: The Polish lords have made their choice: Wenceslaus II, King of Bohemia, a man rich enough to buy loyalty. He is coming north to collect a second crown.

reigns.tagline: The silver king of Bohemia takes Poland too
reigns.previously: The Polish nobles throw out Władysław and invite in Bohemia's king.
paragraphs: Wenceslaus II became King of Bohemia at six, when his father was killed in battle, and spent part of his childhood as a prisoner. He grew up to be one of the richest kings in Europe. The silver mines of Kutná Hora were pouring out metal, and in 1300 he started minting the Prague groschen, a big silver coin that spread far and wide. He even wrote love songs.

He had already taken Kraków in 1291. In 1300 he was crowned King of Poland at Gniezno. To give his rule a Polish face he married Przemysł II's young daughter, and he ran the country through Czech officials. His son was even crowned King of Hungary.
It was the start of a Central European superpower. Then, in June 1305, Wenceslaus died in Prague after a long illness. He was 33.

claims.text: Wenceslaus II wrote love songs that survive in the Codex Manesse.
claims.note: Three songs there are credited to a "King Wenceslas of Bohemia". Most scholars think it's him, but it could be his grandfather.

claims.text: Wenceslaus spent part of his childhood as a prisoner of Otto of Brandenburg.
claims.note: Recorded in Czech chronicles, including the Zbraslav Chronicle.

claims.text: He died of tuberculosis.
claims.note: The chroniclers describe a long wasting illness. Tuberculosis is a modern guess.

reigns.hook: Wenceslaus II is dead. His heir to three kingdoms is a boy of 15 who likes parties. And the little duke Władysław has not given up.

reigns.tagline: The teenage king of three countries, stabbed at 16
reigns.previously: Wenceslaus II dies in 1305 at 33, King of Bohemia and of Poland.
paragraphs: Wenceslaus III was 15 and already a king three times over: Bohemia, Poland and, on paper, Hungary, where he had been crowned at 11. The Hungarian throne was more trouble than it was worth, so he gave up his claim. Czech chroniclers grumbled that he spent his time drinking and partying with young friends.

Poland was slipping away from him. Władysław the Elbow-high was back, taking towns in the south. In summer 1306 Wenceslaus gathered an army to deal with him. On 4 August, at Olomouc in Moravia, he was stabbed to death in his lodgings. He was 16, and the Přemyslid dynasty, which had ruled Bohemia for over 400 years, died with him.
Nobody was ever convicted. In Poland the way was now clear.

claims.text: Wenceslaus III's killer was never identified.
claims.note: A man named Conrad of Botenstein was cut down on the spot and blamed, but chroniclers didn't agree, and the question is still open.

claims.text: Władysław the Elbow-high was behind the murder.
claims.note: Some historians have suspected him, or Habsburg agents. There's no evidence for either.

claims.text: The young king was a heavy-drinking party animal.
claims.note: The Zbraslav Chronicle says so, but its monks wrote with hindsight and liked a moral.

reigns.hook: The last Přemyslid is dead. In Kraków, a tiny, tough Piast duke who has spent years on the run is ready to claim the whole kingdom.

reigns.tagline: The pocket-sized duke who stitched Poland back together
reigns.cameToPower: Took Kraków after the Czechs' fall
reigns.previously: Wenceslaus III is murdered at Olomouc in 1306, the last Přemyslid.
paragraphs: They called him Łokietek, "Elbow-high", because he was famously short. He had been beaten, exiled and written off more than once. In 1306 he took Kraków. Two years later the Teutonic Knights, invited to help defend Gdańsk, seized it themselves and slaughtered many of its people. Then in 1311 the German burghers of Kraków rose against him, led by the town's wójt (chief officer), Albert. He crushed them.

Bit by bit he pieced Poland together. On 20 January 1320 he was crowned King of Poland in Wawel Cathedral, the first coronation there. He married his daughter Elizabeth to the King of Hungary, a match that would matter later. In 1331 he fought the Teutonic Knights at Płowce, a bloody draw the Poles treated as a win.
He died in 1333, in his seventies, leaving a kingdom and one surviving son, Casimir.

claims.text: Hiding from the Bohemians, Łokietek sheltered in a cave near Ojców, and a spider spun a web over the entrance so his pursuers walked past.
claims.note: A local tale attached to the Grota Łokietka cave. A similar story is told about the Prophet Muhammad hiding in a cave.

claims.text: The Teutonic Knights massacred townspeople when they took Gdańsk in 1308.
claims.note: The killing was investigated by a papal inquiry, though the death toll was argued over.

claims.text: Łokietek's coronation in 1320 was the first in Wawel Cathedral.
claims.note: Every later Polish coronation but a few was held there.

reigns.hook: Łokietek is dead. His son Casimir is 22, faces the Teutonic Knights in the north and the Bohemian king's claim to his crown, and inherits a country made largely of wood.

reigns.tagline: The builder king who bargained instead of fighting
reigns.previously: Tiny Łokietek dies, his kingdom finally stitched back together.
paragraphs: Casimir inherited a small kingdom with big enemies: the Teutonic Knights to the north, Bohemia to the west. So he bought peace. He paid the Bohemian king to drop his claim to the Polish crown, let Silesia go, and in 1343 swapped Pomerania for land the Knights had grabbed. Then he turned east and took Red Ruthenia, with Lwów, for Poland.

Peace paid for building. Casimir walled towns, raised dozens of castles and wrote down the law in the Statutes of Wiślica. He confirmed the old rights of the Jews and welcomed them in when much of Europe was driving them out. In 1364 he founded a university in Kraków and hosted a summit of kings there, from the emperor to the King of Cyprus.

His private life was a mess. He married four times, once while his previous wife was still alive, and fathered sons only outside marriage. In September 1370 he fell from his horse while hunting and never recovered. With him the line of Piast kings ended, and by an old family deal the crown went to his sister's son.

claims.text: Casimir found Poland made of wood and left it made of stone.
claims.note: The line comes from Jan Długosz, a century later. The building boom was real, but most of Poland stayed wooden.

claims.text: The merchant Wierzynek threw a feast for the visiting kings in 1364.
claims.note: Told by later chroniclers; the Kraków restaurant that bears his name keeps the story alive. The congress itself is well recorded.

claims.text: Casimir loved a Jewish woman named Esterka and had children by her.
claims.note: Długosz mentions her, but no record of the time does. She became a favourite of later Polish and Jewish folklore.

reigns.hook: The last Piast king is dead with no lawful son. The crown goes to his nephew Louis, already King of Hungary, who has no plans to live in Poland.

reigns.tagline: The Hungarian king who ruled Poland by post
reigns.previously: Casimir the Great dies after a hunting fall, leaving no lawful son.
paragraphs: Louis of Anjou was crowned in Kraków in November 1370, then went home to Hungary as fast as he decently could. He had been King of Hungary since 1342 and saw Poland as a side-dish. He left his mother Elizabeth, Łokietek's daughter, to run it for him. She did not win hearts, and after a riot in Kraków in 1376 killed some of her Hungarian followers, she went home too.

Louis's real problem was that he had only daughters, and Polish law was not keen on queens. So in 1374, at Koszyce, he cut a deal. The nobles would accept one of his girls as heir. In return they would pay almost no tax. It was the first of many bargains in which Polish kings swapped royal power for noble support, and the nobles never forgot the trick.

Louis wanted his daughter Mary and her fiancé, Sigismund of Luxembourg, to take Poland along with Hungary. The Polish lords had other ideas. When Louis died in 1382, they refused to accept another absentee.

claims.text: At Koszyce Louis cut the nobles' tax to a token sum in return for a daughter's succession.
claims.note: The privilege survives. Historians treat it as the start of the nobility's long run of special rights.

claims.text: Louis suffered from leprosy in his last years.
claims.note: He had a long skin disease and stayed out of sight. Some historians have called it leprosy, but the evidence is thin.

reigns.hook: Louis is dead, and he left only daughters. The Polish lords want one of the girls, the younger one, and they want her living in Kraków.

reigns.title: Jadwiga and Jagiełło
reigns.tagline: The girl crowned king, and the pagan duke she married
reigns.previously: Louis dies in Hungary, leaving only daughters.
paragraphs: After two years of wrangling, Louis's youngest daughter Jadwiga arrived in Kraków and was crowned in October 1384. She was about ten, and she was crowned king, not queen, to make it clear she held the throne in her own right. She was already promised to William of Habsburg, but the lords had a bigger idea: marry her to Jogaila, the pagan Grand Duke of Lithuania.

The deal was struck at Krewo in 1385. Jogaila would be baptised, bring Lithuania into the Church and join it to Poland. In February 1386 he was baptised in Kraków as Władysław and married Jadwiga, then was crowned on 4 March. The next year Lithuania, the last pagan state in Europe, began to be baptised. Jadwiga, still a teenager, led an army to win back Red Ruthenia.

The couple waited years for a child. In June 1399 Jadwiga gave birth to a daughter, who lived only a few weeks. Jadwiga died days later. She left her jewels to the Kraków university, which was refounded with them in 1400. Pope John Paul II made her a saint in 1997.

claims.text: Jadwiga grabbed an axe to break down the Wawel gate and run off with William.
claims.note: The story comes from Jan Długosz, writing long after. William did come to Kraków in 1385 and was sent packing.

claims.text: Jadwiga had already consummated her marriage to William.
claims.note: The Habsburg side claimed it to make her match with Jogaila look bigamous. Polish sources deny it, and nothing proves either way.

claims.text: Jadwiga was canonised in 1997.
claims.note: John Paul II declared her a saint at a Mass in Kraków in June 1997.

reigns.hook: Jadwiga is gone, and the deal that made Jagiełło king was built on her. Now a Lithuanian convert must hold the Polish crown on his own.

reigns.tagline: The pagan prince who smashed the Teutonic Knights
reigns.reignEnded: Died of a chill at Gródek
reigns.previously: Queen Jadwiga dies after childbirth, and her baby is already gone.
paragraphs: Without Jadwiga, Jagiełło's hold on Poland looked shaky. He shored it up by marrying Anna of Celje, a granddaughter of Casimir the Great, and by keeping close to his cousin Vytautas, who ran Lithuania for him. The two cousins had one big enemy in common: the Teutonic Knights, the crusading order that held Prussia and kept raiding Lithuania.

On 15 July 1410 they met the Knights at Grunwald. It was one of the biggest battles of medieval Europe. By evening the Grand Master, Ulrich von Jungingen, lay dead with much of his order. Jagiełło failed to take their fortress at Malbork, and the Peace of Thorn in 1411 gave back less than the victory promised. Still, the Knights never fully recovered. In 1413 the Union of Horodło bound Poland and Lithuania tighter.

Jagiełło married four times. Only his last wife, Sophia of Halshany, gave him sons, born when he was an old man. To make sure they would inherit, he granted the nobles new rights, including protection from arrest without trial. He died in 1434, after catching a chill on a spring night out in the woods.

claims.text: Before Grunwald the Grand Master sent Jagiełło two naked swords as a taunt.
claims.note: Told by Jan Długosz, whose father fought in the battle. It fits knightly custom, though his account is the main source.

claims.text: He caught his fatal chill staying out at night to listen to nightingales.
claims.note: Długosz reports it. A long night outdoors is plausible; the nightingales may be decoration.

reigns.hook: The old king is dead. His heir Władysław is a boy of nine, and a bishop is about to run Poland in his name.

reigns.tagline: The boy king who charged the sultan and vanished
reigns.previously: Old Jagiełło dies, leaving two little sons.
paragraphs: Władysław was crowned at nine, and for years the real ruler was Zbigniew Oleśnicki, the Bishop of Kraków. In 1440 the Hungarians, facing the Ottoman threat and a baby heir, offered the teenage king their crown. He took it, which meant a civil war in Hungary and very little time in Poland.

With the Hungarian general John Hunyadi he marched deep into the Balkans in 1443 and did well. In 1444 the sultan offered a truce, and Władysław swore to it. Then the papal legate told him an oath to an infidel did not count, and the crusade marched on. On 10 November 1444, at Varna on the Black Sea, the twenty-year-old king charged the sultan's guard with a handful of knights. He was cut down, and his head was taken as a trophy.
His body was never found. Many Poles refused to believe he was dead, and for three years the throne waited while the country hoped he would turn up.

claims.text: Władysław broke a sworn truce with Sultan Murad II to fight on.
claims.note: The papal legate Cardinal Cesarini released him from the oath. Ottoman and Christian writers agree on the broken truce.

claims.text: He survived Varna and lived out his life on Madeira as a knight called Henrique Alemão.
claims.note: A Portuguese tradition that surfaced much later. There is no good evidence linking the two men.

reigns.hook: No body, no king. Poland waits, and his younger brother Casimir, already ruling Lithuania, is in no hurry to come to Kraków.

reigns.tagline: The patient king who finally broke the Knights
reigns.previously: Władysław of Varna vanishes in battle against the Ottomans.
paragraphs: Casimir had been Grand Duke of Lithuania since he was twelve. He made the Poles wait three years and took their crown in 1447 on terms that kept Lithuania happy. In 1454 the towns of Prussia rose against the Teutonic Knights and asked him to be their lord. He said yes, and a war began that lasted thirteen years.

It went badly at first, and the nobles made him pay for their help with new privileges. Money won it in the end. In 1457 the Knights' own unpaid mercenaries sold Casimir the great castle of Malbork. The Second Peace of Thorn in 1466 gave Poland Gdańsk and Royal Prussia, opening the road to the sea. The Knights kept the rest of Prussia as Poland's vassals.

Casimir and his Habsburg wife Elizabeth had thirteen children. Their eldest son became King of Bohemia and later of Hungary. In Kraków the sculptor Veit Stoss carved the huge altarpiece in St Mary's, and later the king's own tomb. Casimir died in 1492 with plenty of sons to choose from.

claims.text: The Knights' mercenaries sold Malbork to Casimir for unpaid wages.
claims.note: Well documented. The Grand Master had to leave his own headquarters in 1457.

claims.text: Opening Casimir's tomb in 1973 brought a deadly curse.
claims.note: Several of the team died within a few years. Scientists blamed toxic mould found in the tomb.

reigns.hook: Casimir dies with a house full of sons. One already rules Bohemia. Now the nobles must pick a Polish king, and they choose the restless one, John Albert.

reigns.tagline: The warrior king whose army died in the forest
reigns.previously: Casimir IV dies at Grodno; his sons now rule half of central Europe.
paragraphs: Jan Olbracht to the Poles, John Albert was elected king in 1492 while his brother Alexander took Lithuania. He had been taught by the Italian humanist Callimachus and liked big plans. His reign is when the Sejm, Poland's parliament, settled into two houses: a Senate of great lords and bishops, and a chamber of envoys for the gentry.

The gentry got their reward in 1496. The Statute of Piotrków limited how peasants could leave the land and stopped townsmen buying country estates. It was a big step towards tying peasants to their lords. In 1497 John Albert led a great army into Moldavia. It failed to take Suceava, and on the way home it was ambushed in the Bukovina forest and badly mauled.
Tatar raids followed the defeat, and his plans for a crusade came to nothing. He died suddenly at Toruń in 1501, unmarried and without children, at 41.

claims.text: "In King Olbracht's day the nobles perished."
claims.note: A Polish rhyming saying about the Bukovina disaster. The defeat was real, but the rhyme overstates the losses.

claims.text: Callimachus wrote secret advice telling the king to crush the nobles' freedoms.
claims.note: The so-called Counsels of Callimachus survive only in later copies, and most historians think they are a forgery.

reigns.hook: John Albert dies childless. The crown goes to his brother Alexander, who is fighting Moscow while married to the Grand Prince of Moscow's daughter.

reigns.tagline: The king who promised to make no law alone
reigns.previously: John Albert dies suddenly at Toruń, unmarried and childless.
paragraphs: Alexander had been Grand Duke of Lithuania since 1492, and Lithuania was his real job. To keep the peace he married Helena, daughter of Ivan III of Moscow. It did not work. Ivan attacked anyway, beat the Lithuanians on the Vedrosha river in 1500 and kept a big slice of their land. Helena, meanwhile, stayed proudly Orthodox.

As King of Poland he was short of money and short of friends. At the Sejm in Radom in 1505 he agreed to the act known as Nihil novi, "nothing new": no new law without the consent of the Senate and the envoys of the gentry. That made the gentry partners in power. The same year, Jan Łaski's great collection of Polish laws was ordered into print.
By 1506 Alexander was paralysed and dying. Lying in Vilnius, he heard that his army had beaten the Crimean Tatars at Kletsk. He died days later, in August 1506, without children.

claims.text: The Nihil novi act of 1505 barred new laws without the Sejm's consent.
claims.note: The text survives. Historians see it as a founding rule of the nobles' democracy.

claims.text: Queen Helena refused to give up her Orthodox faith.
claims.note: Her father insisted on it in the marriage deal, and she kept to it all her life.

reigns.tagline: The old king of Poland's golden age
reigns.previously: Alexander dies in Vilnius, paralysed and childless.
paragraphs: Sigismund waited a long time for a throne and then held it for over forty years. In 1518 he married Bona Sforza, a duchess from Milan with strong opinions and Italian tastes. Italian artists rebuilt Wawel as a Renaissance palace. The Sigismund Chapel rose beside the cathedral, and in 1520 the great Sigismund Bell was hung there.

In 1525 Albrecht of Hohenzollern, the last Grand Master of the Teutonic Knights in Prussia, turned Lutheran, shut down the order there and knelt in Kraków's market square to receive Prussia as a duchy from Sigismund. In 1543 Copernicus, a royal subject, published his book putting the sun at the centre. It was Poland's golden age.

Not everyone was happy. In 1537 the gentry gathered near Lwów for a war, then spent their time protesting against Bona and the king's reforms. They went home without a fight, and people called it the Hen War, since all they killed was the local poultry. Sigismund had his son crowned in his own lifetime. He died in 1548, at 81.

claims.text: Bona brought vegetables to Poland, and Poles still call soup greens "włoszczyzna", the Italian stuff.
claims.note: The word is real and the queen's Italian kitchen is attested. That she introduced the vegetables herself is folklore.

claims.text: The Hen War got its name because the gentry ate the local hens and did nothing else.
claims.note: The mocking name was used at the time. The protest itself was a real political crisis.

reigns.hook: The old king dies at 81. His son is already crowned, but he is hiding a secret wife whom his mother hates, and the Sejm is about to find out.

reigns.tagline: The last Jagiellon, who married for love
reigns.previously: Sigismund the Old dies in Kraków, aged 81.
paragraphs: Sigismund Augustus was crowned as a boy, while his father lived. When he took over, he dropped a bombshell: he had secretly married Barbara Radziwiłł, a Lithuanian widow from a pushy magnate family. His mother Bona and the Sejm demanded he get rid of her. He refused, and in 1550 Barbara was crowned queen. Within months she was dead.

His third marriage, to a Habsburg, was miserable, and he had no children. So he spent his energy on a bigger project. In 1569 the Union of Lublin merged Poland and Lithuania into one Commonwealth, with one elected king and one Sejm, while each kept its own army, treasury and laws. It was the largest state in Europe.
He loved books and collected the great Flemish tapestries that still hang in Wawel. He died at Knyszyn in July 1572. The male Jagiellon line died with him, and there was no plan for what came next.

claims.text: Queen Bona had Barbara Radziwiłł poisoned.
claims.note: Gossip said so at the time. Barbara's long illness fits a cancer much better, and no proof was ever found.

claims.text: The magician Twardowski raised Barbara's ghost in a mirror for the grieving king.
claims.note: A popular legend; Twardowski himself is half folklore. A mirror said to be his is shown in a church at Węgrów.

claims.text: The Union of Lublin created a single Commonwealth with one elected king.
claims.note: The act of union of 1 July 1569 survives and was in force until the partitions.

reigns.tagline: The French prince who fled his new kingdom by night
reigns.previously: Sigismund Augustus dies childless. The Jagiellon line is over.
paragraphs: With no Jagiellon left, the Poles tried something new. Every nobleman, rich or poor, could ride to a field near Warsaw and vote for the next king, and tens of thousands came. In May 1573 they chose Henry of Valois, younger brother of the French king Charles IX. The nobles, the szlachta, set terms first. Henry had to sign the Henrician Articles: no naming his own heir, a Sejm (parliament) every two years, and no war or new taxes without its say.

He reached Poland early in 1574 and was crowned at Wawel in February. He spoke no Polish, disliked the cold and kept dodging the marriage everyone expected, to Anna Jagiellon, the old king's sister, who was almost thirty years his senior. Then came news that Charles IX had died on 30 May. Henry was now King of France as well, and he knew which crown he wanted.

On the night of 18 June he slipped out of Wawel with a few French friends and galloped for the border. Courtiers raced after him, and by most accounts one caught up with him in Silesia and begged him to turn back. Henry kept riding. He had spent less than five months in Poland. The Poles gave him a deadline to return, and when it passed they declared the throne empty.

claims.text: A Polish nobleman caught up with the fleeing king near the border and begged him to come back.
claims.note: The chase is well recorded; who reached him, where, and what was said differ from one account to the next.

claims.text: Henry brought the table fork to Poland, or took the fork home to France.
claims.note: A tidy story in both countries. Forks were already known in Italy and at some northern courts, and nobody at the time credits Henry.

claims.text: Henry's Articles bound every king of Poland after him.
claims.note: The text survives, and each elected king swore to it until the Commonwealth ended in 1795.

reigns.hook: The throne is empty again, and this time the electors split. The senators want the Holy Roman Emperor. The crowd of nobles shout for a tough soldier-prince from Transylvania who will marry Anna Jagiellon.

reigns.tagline: The Transylvanian who beat Ivan the Terrible
reigns.cameToPower: Elected by the mass of nobles
reigns.previously: Henry of Valois bolts for France. The Poles declare the throne empty.
paragraphs: In December 1575 the senators named the Emperor Maximilian II king. The mass of the nobles would not have it and chose Stephen Báthory, Prince of Transylvania, on condition that he marry Anna Jagiellon. Báthory moved fast. On 1 May 1576 he married Anna in Kraków and the two were crowned side by side the same day. Maximilian died that autumn before he could fight for the crown.

Rich Gdańsk had backed the emperor and shut its gates. Báthory beat its army in 1577 and besieged the city until it paid a heavy fine and submitted. Then he turned on Muscovy, which had been grabbing Livonia. He took Polotsk in 1579 and Velikiye Luki in 1580, then besieged Pskov through the winter of 1581–82. Pskov held, but Ivan the Terrible gave up his Livonian conquests in the peace of 1582.

Báthory founded the university at Vilnius in 1579, trusted his Hungarian infantry and dreamed of even bigger wars against the Turks. He never got them. He fell ill and died at Grodno in December 1586, aged 53, leaving no children.

claims.text: Báthory never learned Polish and spoke Latin to the nobles.
claims.note: Often repeated. He certainly did business in Latin, which most nobles understood; how much Polish he picked up is unclear.

claims.text: Pskov held out against Báthory's army for months.
claims.note: Described on both sides, including the Russian 'Tale of Stefan Batory's Coming to Pskov'.

claims.text: He turned the Jesuit college in Vilnius into a university in 1579.
claims.note: His charter survives, and the pope confirmed it the same year.

reigns.hook: Another empty throne, another split vote. One party wants an Austrian archduke. The other wants Anna's nephew, a Swedish prince who is a Jagiellon on his mother's side.

reigns.tagline: The king who lost Sweden and moved Poland's capital
reigns.cameToPower: Elected; his rival beaten in battle
reigns.previously: Stephen Báthory dies at Grodno, leaving no heir.
paragraphs: Sigismund was born in a Swedish prison, son of Duke John of Finland and the Polish princess Catherine Jagiellon. In 1587 one party of Polish nobles elected him king. Another chose Archduke Maximilian of Austria, but Chancellor Jan Zamoyski beat the archduke at Byczyna in 1588 and took him prisoner. In 1592 Sigismund inherited Sweden too. He was a devout Catholic, and the Lutheran Swedes never trusted him.

His uncle Charles led the opposition, beat him in battle in 1598, and in 1599 the Swedes deposed him. Sigismund never stopped claiming Sweden, which meant decades of war. After a fire at Wawel he moved the court to Warsaw, which slowly became the capital. Hetman Chodkiewicz crushed a far bigger Swedish army at Kircholm in 1605, and a nobles' revolt led by Mikołaj Zebrzydowski was beaten in 1607.

Then came Russia's Time of Troubles. Hetman Żółkiewski smashed a Russian army at Klushino in 1610, and Polish troops held the Moscow Kremlin until 1612. Sigismund wanted the Russian throne for himself, not his son, and the chance slipped away. He died in 1632 after almost 45 years as king. His son put him on a column in Warsaw, where he still stands.

claims.text: Sigismund dabbled in alchemy, and an experiment started the Wawel fire.
claims.note: The alchemist Michael Sendivogius did work for him. Blaming the fire on royal experiments is later gossip.

claims.text: Polish troops held the Moscow Kremlin from 1610 to 1612.
claims.note: Polish and Russian sources agree. The garrison's surrender is still marked in Russia as Unity Day.

claims.text: Sigismund's column in Warsaw was put up by his son Władysław IV in 1644.
claims.note: Recorded at the time; it is the oldest secular monument in Warsaw.

reigns.hook: The old king is dead. His son Władysław is the easy choice: a popular soldier who was once elected Tsar of Russia and never got to wear the crown.

reigns.tagline: The tsar who never reigned and the king who dreamed of war
reigns.previously: Sigismund III dies in Warsaw after almost 45 years as king.
paragraphs: Władysław had a gift his father lacked: people liked him. In 1610, aged 15, he was elected Tsar by the Moscow boyars, but his father would not let him go or turn Orthodox, and the Russians chose Michael Romanov instead. In 1632 the Poles elected Władysław without a fight. Moscow chose that moment to besiege Smolensk. He marched east, trapped the Russian army and made it surrender.

At the Peace of Polyanovka in 1634 he kept Smolensk and gave up his claim to be tsar. He loved music and had Italian operas staged at the royal castle in Warsaw. He married twice, first the Habsburg princess Cecilia Renata, then the French Marie Louise Gonzaga. His great dream was a war on the Ottoman Turks, and he quietly got the Cossacks of Ukraine ready for it. The Sejm refused to pay.

His only son died in 1647, aged seven. The next spring a Cossack officer named Bohdan Khmelnytsky rose in revolt and beat the first Polish forces sent against him. Władysław died on 20 May 1648, with the great rising only just beginning.

claims.text: The boyars of Moscow elected Władysław tsar in 1610.
claims.note: The agreement made with Hetman Żółkiewski survives. He never went to Moscow and was never crowned.

claims.text: Władysław secretly promised the Cossacks more rights if they fought the Turks.
claims.note: Historians argue over how far he went. The Cossacks later said the king had been on their side.

reigns.hook: The king is dead and Ukraine is burning. The nobles turn to his younger half-brother, John Casimir, who has already been a Jesuit and a cardinal.

reigns.tagline: The ex-cardinal who watched Poland drown in the Deluge
reigns.cameToPower: Elected in the middle of a war
reigns.previously: Władysław IV dies just as Khmelnytsky's Cossacks rise in Ukraine.
paragraphs: John Casimir had already been a Jesuit novice and a cardinal. He gave both up, won the election in November 1648 and married his late brother's widow, Marie Louise Gonzaga, who became the sharpest mind at court. He inherited a war. Khmelnytsky's Cossacks and their Crimean Tatar allies fought the Poles for years, and in 1654 Khmelnytsky put his part of Ukraine under the Russian tsar.

In 1652 one deputy, Władysław Siciński, broke up the Sejm with a single word: veto. Under this "free veto", one noble could wreck a whole session. Then in 1655 Charles X of Sweden invaded. Magnates and whole provinces went over to him, and the king fled to Silesia. Poles call it the Deluge.

The monastery of Jasna Góra held out against a Swedish siege, and the tide turned. At Lwów in 1656 John Casimir vowed to make the Virgin Mary Queen of Poland and to ease the lot of the peasants. The Swedes were driven out, but Kiev and Ukraine east of the Dnieper were lost to Russia. His wife died in 1667. A year later he abdicated, and he died in France in 1672.

claims.text: The Virgin Mary saved Jasna Góra from the Swedes.
claims.note: The miracle story comes from the prior, Augustyn Kordecki, whose account came out in 1658. The siege and the defence were real.

claims.text: John Casimir warned that Russia, Brandenburg and Austria would one day carve Poland up.
claims.note: He did warn the Sejm along these lines in 1661. Later writers tied it to his abdication and sharpened it with hindsight.

claims.text: In 1652 a single deputy broke up the Sejm for the first time.
claims.note: Siciński's veto is well documented. The device was used dozens of times afterwards.

reigns.hook: The last Vasa has gone. The nobles, fed up with foreign candidates, pick a Pole: the shy son of a famous warlord. When he hears the news, he bursts into tears.

reigns.tagline: The king who wept when he got the job
reigns.previously: John II Casimir abdicates and leaves for France.
paragraphs: Michał Korybut Wiśniowiecki was the son of Prince Jeremi Wiśniowiecki, the ferocious magnate who had fought Khmelnytsky's Cossacks. Michał himself was poor, quiet and nobody's favourite. But in 1669 the crowd of nobles at the election were tired of French and German candidates and shouted for a Pole. They got him. He married the emperor's sister, Eleonora of Austria, which annoyed the pro-French party.

His reign was one long quarrel. A powerful faction, including Hetman John Sobieski, plotted to depose him. In 1672 the Ottoman army took the fortress of Kamieniec Podolski, and at Buczacz the king's envoys signed away Podolia and agreed to pay the sultan tribute. The Sejm refused to swallow that, and the war went on.
Michał fell ill and died at Lwów on 10 November 1673, aged 33. The very next day, with no idea that the king was dead, Sobieski smashed the Ottoman army at Khotyn.

claims.text: Michał burst into tears when told he had been elected.
claims.note: A story passed on by diarists of the time and repeated ever since. It fits his meek reputation, which may be why it stuck.

claims.text: Sobieski's victory at Khotyn came the day after the king died.
claims.note: Both dates, 10 and 11 November 1673, are well documented. News simply had not reached the camp.

reigns.hook: The hero of Khotyn rides home to a kingdom with no king. The nobles know exactly whom they want.

reigns.tagline: The king who charged down the hill to save Vienna
reigns.previously: King Michał dies, and the next day Sobieski wins at Khotyn.
paragraphs: John Sobieski was a big, brave, clever soldier from a well-off noble family. Fresh from Khotyn, he was elected king in May 1674. He was also hopelessly in love with his French wife, Marie Casimire, whom he called Marysieńka. His letters to her from the camp, full of longing, jokes and battle news, are still read today.

His big moment came in 1683. A huge Ottoman army under Grand Vizier Kara Mustafa was besieging Vienna. Sobieski marched south and took command of the relief army. On 12 September 1683, after a day of hard fighting, he led a vast cavalry charge down the slopes of the Kahlenberg, with the winged hussars in front. The Ottoman army broke and fled, leaving its camp and its treasure behind.

Back home the glory faded. Wars to win back Podolia went nowhere, the Sejm squabbled and his own family fought over the succession. He built a lovely palace at Wilanów, just outside Warsaw, and died there in June 1696. His son Jakub hoped to follow him. The nobles had other ideas.

claims.text: After Vienna, Sobieski wrote to the pope: 'We came, we saw, God conquered.'
claims.note: The line is famous and usually tied to his letter to Innocent XI, but the exact wording is hard to pin to a surviving original.

claims.text: The bagel, or the croissant, was invented to celebrate Sobieski's victory.
claims.note: Bagels are recorded in Kraków decades before 1683, and the croissant story only appears much later.

claims.text: He wrote hundreds of love letters to Marysieńka.
claims.note: The letters survive and have been published many times.

reigns.hook: Sobieski is dead, and the nobles want no more Sobieskis. The prize goes to a German prince who changes his religion to win it, and who is said to bend horseshoes with his bare hands.

reigns.tagline: The strongman who lost his crown, then took it back
reigns.previously: Sobieski dies at Wilanów. His family squabble over the crown.
paragraphs: Frederick Augustus, Elector of Saxony, wanted to be a king. In 1697 he turned Catholic, spent a fortune on votes and was elected by part of the nobility; a larger party had chosen the French Prince of Conti. Augustus simply got to Kraków first with Saxon troops and was crowned. Conti sailed to Gdańsk, saw how things stood and went home.

In 1700 Augustus joined Russia and Denmark in a war on Sweden, the Great Northern War. It went badly. Charles XII of Sweden invaded Poland, set up a king of his own and then marched into Saxony itself. In 1706 Augustus had to give up the Polish crown. When Peter the Great crushed Charles at Poltava in 1709, Augustus came straight back.

The war turned Poland into a playground for foreign armies. At the Silent Sejm of 1717, so called because hardly anyone was allowed to speak, the Polish army was capped at a small size with Russia as go-between. Augustus poured money into Dresden, where his chemists cracked the secret of porcelain and founded Meissen. He died in Warsaw in 1733.

claims.text: Augustus could bend horseshoes with his bare hands.
claims.note: A favourite story of his own day, told to show off his strength. Nobody can check it.

claims.text: He fathered over 300 illegitimate children.
claims.note: The giant figure is 18th-century gossip. He acknowledged only a handful, the most famous being the general Maurice de Saxe.

claims.text: He signed away the Polish crown at Altranstädt in 1706.
claims.note: The treaty with Charles XII survives. He tore it up after Poltava.

reigns.hook: Go back to 1704. With Augustus still fighting, Charles XII decides Poland needs a new king, and he has picked a cultured young nobleman named Stanisław Leszczyński.

reigns.tagline: Twice a king of Poland, and twice chased out
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Rival king, chosen by Charles XII
reigns.previously: Augustus the Strong dies. But rewind to 1704 and his Swedish rival.
paragraphs: Stanisław Leszczyński was a cultured, good-natured noble of 26 when Charles XII of Sweden chose him to replace Augustus. A small assembly near Warsaw, guarded by Swedish troops, elected him in July 1704, and he was crowned the next year. He stayed king exactly as long as the Swedish army stood behind him. When Peter the Great destroyed that army at Poltava in 1709, Stanisław had to run.

He ended up in exile in Alsace, short of money and nearly forgotten. Then came a stroke of luck: in 1725 his daughter Marie married the young Louis XV and became Queen of France. When Augustus died in 1733, French money made Stanisław a candidate again. He crossed Germany in secret, reached Warsaw and was elected in September 1733.

Russia and Austria would not have it. A Russian army chased him to Gdańsk and besieged the city in 1734. Stanisław got out before it fell. In the peace deal he gave up Poland for the Duchy of Lorraine, his for life. He spent 30 happy years there, building and writing, and died in 1766 at 88 after his dressing gown caught fire.

claims.text: Stanisław escaped besieged Gdańsk disguised as a peasant.
claims.note: He certainly slipped out before the city surrendered. The colourful disguise comes from his own and his friends' later retellings.

claims.text: He died after his dressing gown caught fire by the hearth.
claims.note: Reported at Lunéville at the time. He lingered for some days with his burns before he died.

claims.text: His daughter Marie became Queen of France.
claims.note: She married Louis XV in 1725 and was queen for over 40 years.

reigns.hook: Stanisław has fled Gdańsk. The Russians already have their own man on the throne: Augustus the Strong's son, who would much rather be in Dresden.

reigns.tagline: The absentee king of fine paintings and broken parliaments
reigns.previously: Stanisław flees Gdańsk. Russia's candidate, Augustus III, takes over.
paragraphs: Augustus III got Poland the way his father got it back: with foreign help. A small group of nobles elected him on 5 October 1733 while a Russian army stood by, and he was crowned in Kraków in January 1734. The Russians then besieged Gdańsk and drove out his rival. This was the War of the Polish Succession, and it was Poland's neighbours who settled it.

Augustus much preferred Dresden. He loved hunting, opera and pictures, and he bought Raphael's Sistine Madonna for his gallery there. The hard work he left to his minister, Count Heinrich von Brühl, famous for his lavish wardrobe. In Poland the great magnate families ran their own politics, and almost every Sejm of the reign broke up without passing a single law.

Still, there were 30 years of peace inside Poland, and the nobles remembered them fondly. When Prussia overran Saxony in 1756, Augustus spent most of the Seven Years' War in Warsaw. He went home in 1763 and died in Dresden on 5 October, 30 years to the day after his election.

claims.text: Nobles summed up the age: 'Under the Saxon king, eat, drink and loosen your belt.'
claims.note: A genuine old Polish saying. It captures how the era was remembered, not hard history.

claims.text: Only one Sejm in his 30 years managed to finish its work.
claims.note: The usual count says only the 1736 'pacification' Sejm passed laws; historians differ on how to count the rest.

reigns.hook: Augustus III is dead. Catherine the Great of Russia already knows who the next King of Poland will be: a charming young Pole who was once her lover.

reigns.tagline: The last king, who watched his country vanish
reigns.previously: Augustus III dies in Dresden. Catherine the Great picks the next king.
paragraphs: Stanisław Poniatowski was clever, charming and well read. As a young diplomat in St Petersburg he had an affair with the Grand Duchess Catherine. Once she was Empress, she made him King of Poland, with Russian troops close to the election field in 1764. She expected a puppet. He wanted to reform the country, which made Russia angry and many Polish nobles suspicious.

Conservative nobles formed the Confederation of Bar in 1768 and fought both Russia and the king. In 1771 some of them kidnapped him in Warsaw, but he talked one captor round and got away. In 1772 Russia, Prussia and Austria took almost a third of the country in the First Partition. Stanisław kept going. He set up the Commission of National Education, hosted Thursday dinners for writers and filled Warsaw with art.

The Great Sejm passed the Constitution of 3 May 1791, one of the first modern written constitutions anywhere. Magnates of the Targowica Confederation called in Russia, and the king gave way. The Second Partition followed in 1793. Kościuszko's uprising of 1794 was crushed, and in 1795 the rest of Poland was shared out. On 25 November Stanisław abdicated. He died in St Petersburg in 1798.

claims.text: Catherine the Great made her former lover King of Poland.
claims.note: Stanisław's own memoirs and Catherine's writings both describe the affair, and her backing for him in 1764 is well documented.

claims.text: Kidnapped by Bar confederates, he talked one of his captors into letting him go.
claims.note: Well documented; the kidnappers were later put on trial in Warsaw.

claims.text: The 3 May Constitution was Europe's first modern written constitution.
claims.note: Widely said in Poland. It did come months before France's, though Corsica's constitution of 1755 is sometimes counted as earlier.

reigns.hook: There is no king and no Poland. Russia, Prussia and Austria have split the land three ways. The Poles will spend 123 years trying to get it back.

reigns.title: The Partitions
reigns.tagline: 123 years without a country, and never giving up
reigns.previously: Stanisław August abdicates. Poland disappears from the map.
paragraphs: After 1795 there was no Poland on the map. Russia held the east, Prussia the west and Warsaw, Austria the south with Kraków. Poles kept fighting anyway. In 1797 Polish legions formed in Italy to fight alongside Napoleon, and Józef Wybicki wrote them a marching song: "Poland has not yet perished, so long as we live." It is now the national anthem.

Napoleon set up a Duchy of Warsaw in 1807. Its hero, Prince Józef Poniatowski, the last king's nephew, drowned covering the retreat from Leipzig in 1813. In 1815 the Congress of Vienna handed most of the duchy to Russia as a Kingdom of Poland, with the tsar as king. Poles rose in November 1830 and again in January 1863. Both times Russia crushed them, with hangings and exile to Siberia.

After 1831 thousands went west in the Great Emigration, among them Chopin and the poet Mickiewicz. At home, Russia and Prussia pushed their own languages in schools and offices. Maria Skłodowska, born in Warsaw, had to study in secret before winning two Nobel Prizes in France. Then the First World War set the three empires against each other. By late 1918 all three had collapsed, and on 11 November Poland was free.

claims.text: 'Dąbrowski's Mazurka' was first sung by the Polish legions in Italy in 1797.
claims.note: Wybicki wrote it at Reggio Emilia in July 1797. It became the official anthem in 1927.

claims.text: Prince Józef Poniatowski drowned in the River Elster after Leipzig.
claims.note: Wounded, he rode into the river on 19 October 1813. His famous last words about honour are probably later polish.

claims.text: Maria Skłodowska studied at Warsaw's secret 'Flying University'.
claims.note: She described it herself: an underground college that moved from flat to flat to dodge the tsar's police.

reigns.hook: Poland is back, but its borders are unsettled and enemies circle on every side. Power falls to a former train robber who spent years in Russian and German hands: Józef Piłsudski.

reigns.cameToPower: Handed power by the Regency Council
reigns.previously: After 123 years of partition, Poland is back on the map.
paragraphs: No more kings now. From here we follow whoever really held power, and in 1918 that was Józef Piłsudski. Born near Vilnius in 1867, he did five years in Siberia as a young man, became a socialist revolutionary, and in 1908 helped rob a Russian mail train at Bezdany for party funds. In the First World War he raised Polish Legions, then fell out with the Germans and landed in a Magdeburg prison. Freed in November 1918, he came home to Warsaw a hero.

As Chief of State he fought on every border. In 1920 the Red Army reached the gates of Warsaw, and in August Piłsudski's counter-attack smashed it, the "Miracle on the Vistula". In 1922 he handed over to an elected president, Gabriel Narutowicz, who was shot dead by a nationalist fanatic within days. Fed up with squabbling politicians, Piłsudski marched on Warsaw in May 1926 and seized power in a three-day coup.

He refused the presidency. He didn't need it. As "the Marshal" and minister of war he ran the country from behind the scenes, and jailed opposition leaders when they got in his way. He died on 12 May 1935. His body went to Wawel with the kings; his heart went to Vilnius, buried with his mother.

claims.text: Piłsudski took part in the armed robbery of a Russian mail train at Bezdany in 1908.
claims.note: He led the raid himself; the woman who became his second wife, Aleksandra Szczerbińska, was among the plotters. The money went to his fighting organisation.

claims.text: The 1920 victory was a miracle, or the work of French advisers rather than Piłsudski.
claims.note: The phrase was spread by his political enemies to deny him credit. Historians give the plan to Piłsudski and his chief of staff Tadeusz Rozwadowski; French general Weygand himself said the victory was Polish.

claims.text: His heart is buried in Vilnius in his mother's grave.
claims.note: It was placed in the Rasos cemetery in 1936 under a black granite slab, as he had asked.

reigns.hook: The Marshal is dead and nobody can fill his boots. His colonels inherit a state built around one man, with Hitler to the west and Stalin to the east.

reigns.title: The Colonels
reigns.tagline: The Marshal's men, a new constitution and no way out
reigns.previously: Piłsudski dies. His heart goes to Vilnius, his body to Wawel.
paragraphs: Weeks before he died, Piłsudski's camp pushed through a new constitution in April 1935 that put a strong president at the top. Without him, power split three ways. President Ignacy Mościcki, a chemistry professor, kept the office. General Edward Rydz-Śmigły took the army and became a Marshal in 1936. Józef Beck, a colonel, ran foreign policy. The regime was called Sanation, from the Latin for healing.

It was a hard, nervous time. The opposition was squeezed, and nationalist pressure on Jews grew, with separate benches for Jewish students at some universities. Abroad, Beck tried to balance between Berlin and Moscow and tie Poland to neither. When Germany carved up Czechoslovakia in 1938, Poland sent an ultimatum and grabbed the Zaolzie district too.

Then Hitler turned on Poland, demanding Danzig and a road across Polish land. Britain promised to defend Poland on 31 March 1939. On 5 May Beck told the Sejm no: peace was precious, but honour had no price. In August, Hitler and Stalin signed a pact with a secret clause splitting Poland between them.

claims.text: Beck refused Hitler's demands in a speech saying honour was the one thing without price.
claims.note: He spoke to the Sejm on 5 May 1939. The speech was hugely popular in Poland and is still quoted.

claims.text: Poland took part in the break-up of Czechoslovakia.
claims.note: After the Munich deal, Warsaw issued an ultimatum on 30 September 1938 and Polish troops entered Zaolzie days later.

claims.text: Piłsudski picked Rydz-Śmigły as his successor.
claims.note: He had marked Rydz-Śmigły out as the next head of the army, but he named no political heir, which is why power split three ways.

reigns.hook: Before dawn on 1 September 1939, the German battleship Schleswig-Holstein opens fire on the Polish depot at Westerplatte. Six years of war begin.

reigns.title: War and Occupation
reigns.tagline: Invaded from both sides, and the Holocaust on Polish soil
reigns.previously: Beck says no to Hitler. Hitler and Stalin secretly carve it up.
paragraphs: Germany invaded on 1 September 1939. The small garrison at Westerplatte held out for a week. On 17 September the Soviet Union invaded from the east, as agreed with Hitler. Warsaw surrendered on 28 September. A government-in-exile formed, first in France, then in London. Both occupiers set out to destroy Poland as a nation. The Soviets deported hundreds of thousands, and in 1940 their secret police shot about 22,000 Polish officers and others at Katyn and other sites.

Germany ran a regime of mass terror: executions, expulsions, forced labour. It also carried out the Holocaust. About three million Polish Jews were murdered, most of them in death camps that Germany built and ran in occupied Poland, among them Auschwitz-Birkenau and Treblinka. In April 1943 the fighters of the Warsaw Ghetto rose up against the Germans. The Polish underground army grew into one of the largest in occupied Europe.

In July 1943 the exile leader, General Sikorski, was killed in a plane crash at Gibraltar. Polish troops took Monte Cassino in May 1944. On 1 August 1944 the Home Army rose in Warsaw; after 63 days it surrendered, at least 150,000 civilians were dead, and Germany then razed the city. The Red Army stood across the Vistula. At Yalta in February 1945, the Allies agreed to move Poland's borders west. Close to six million Polish citizens died in the war.

claims.text: The Soviet Union carried out the Katyn massacre and blamed it on Germany for nearly 50 years.
claims.note: The NKVD shot the prisoners in April and May 1940. Moscow admitted it only in April 1990, and released the key documents in 1992.

claims.text: Auschwitz, Treblinka and the other death camps were German camps.
claims.note: They were set up and run by Nazi Germany in occupied Poland. Calling them "Polish camps" is simply wrong.

claims.text: Stalin halted the Red Army so the Germans would crush the Warsaw Uprising.
claims.note: His offensive had stalled after a long advance, but he also refused for weeks to let Allied supply planes land on Soviet-held airfields. Historians still argue over how far it was a choice.

reigns.hook: Germany surrenders on 8 May 1945. Poland is on the winning side, but the Red Army stays, and Stalin's chosen men are already in charge in Warsaw.

reigns.tagline: Moscow's man and Poland's Stalinist years
reigns.previously: The war ends. Poland is shifted west, with the Red Army still there.
paragraphs: Bolesław Bierut was a self-taught working man from Lublin who became a communist, spent years in the Soviet Union and sat in a Polish jail in the 1930s. From the start of 1944 he chaired the communists' National Council, and when the war ended he headed the new state. A few exiles came home to join the government, but the communists held the police and the guns.

The 1946 referendum and the 1947 election were both rigged. The parliament made Bierut president, and the opposition leader Mikołajczyk fled abroad. In 1948 Bierut pushed aside his rival Gomułka, later jailing him, and led the new ruling party. Stalinism followed: show trials, torture, collective farms. Witold Pilecki, who had let himself be sent to Auschwitz to report on it, was executed in 1948. The Primate, Cardinal Wyszyński, was locked up in 1953.

Stalin's "gift", the giant Palace of Culture, rose over Warsaw. In February 1956 Bierut went to Moscow for the Soviet party congress, where Khrushchev denounced Stalin in a secret speech. Bierut fell ill there and never came home alive. He died on 12 March 1956.

claims.text: The 1946 referendum results were faked.
claims.note: Archive research has shown the published figures were made up; most voters had actually rejected at least one of the communists' questions.

claims.text: Bierut was poisoned in Moscow.
claims.note: There is no evidence. The rumour, and the Polish joke that he "went in a fur coat and came back in a box", grew from the timing, days after the Secret Speech.

claims.text: Witold Pilecki volunteered to be sent to Auschwitz.
claims.note: He got himself caught in a Warsaw round-up in 1940, organised resistance in the camp, escaped in 1943 and wrote detailed reports.

reigns.hook: Bierut's death cracks the ice. In June, workers in Poznań take to the streets, and the party turns to a man it once threw in prison.

reigns.tagline: The reformer who faced down Khrushchev, then went sour
reigns.previously: Bierut dies in Moscow, days after Khrushchev denounces Stalin.
paragraphs: Edward Ochab led the party for a few months after Bierut. In June 1956 the workers of Poznań rose up, and the army crushed them, killing dozens. The party needed someone people might trust. It found Władysław Gomułka, a former fitter with a limp from a police bullet, who had led the wartime communist underground and spent over three years in jail under Bierut.

On 19 October Khrushchev flew into Warsaw uninvited while Soviet tanks moved. Gomułka stood his ground, and two days later he was party leader. Collective farms were broken up, the Cardinal was freed, and huge crowds cheered. The thaw didn't last. In 1968 he crushed student protests and led a campaign against "Zionists" that drove most of Poland's remaining Jews out of the country. Polish troops joined the invasion of Czechoslovakia.

In December 1970 he signed a treaty with West Germany accepting Poland's new western border. Days later his government raised food prices just before Christmas. The shipyards of Gdańsk, Gdynia and Szczecin went on strike, and troops and police opened fire. Officially 41 people were killed. Gomułka was out on 20 December.

claims.text: Gomułka faced down Khrushchev in October 1956.
claims.note: Khrushchev arrived with top Soviet generals on 19 October; after tense talks he backed off, and Gomułka was elected party leader on 21 October.

claims.text: West German Chancellor Willy Brandt fell to his knees at the Warsaw Ghetto memorial.
claims.note: It happened on 7 December 1970, the day the treaty was signed. The photos went round the world.

claims.text: "Janek Wiśniewski", the young man carried dead on a door in Gdynia, was a real victim with that name.
claims.note: The name came from a protest song. The victim in the famous scene was 18-year-old Zbigniew Godlewski.

reigns.tagline: Borrowed billions, a tiny Fiat and a Polish pope
reigns.previously: Troops fire on striking shipyard workers. Gomułka is forced out.
paragraphs: Edward Gierek grew up among Polish miners in France and went down the pit at 13. He fought in the Belgian resistance, came home in 1948 and ran Silesia like a showcase. In January 1971 he went to the Gdańsk shipyard himself and asked the strikers for help. Then he went shopping, with Western loans. New factories, steelworks, flats and motorways went up. From 1973 Poles could buy their own car, the little Fiat 126p, the "Maluch".

It was built on credit. By the late 1970s the debts were huge and the shops were empty again. A price rise in 1976 set off riots in Radom and Ursus, and dissidents set up a committee to help the jailed workers. In 1978 the Archbishop of Kraków, Karol Wojtyła, became Pope John Paul II. In June 1979 he toured Poland and millions came out to hear him. People saw how many of them there were.

In August 1980 the Lenin Shipyard in Gdańsk went on strike, and the whole coast followed. On 31 August the government signed the Gdańsk Agreement, allowing a free trade union. Solidarity was born. Days later Gierek, ill and blamed for everything, was replaced.

claims.text: Gierek asked "Will you help?" and the shipyard workers shouted back "We will help!"
claims.note: He did ask, but the famous answering chant is doubted; some participants said the crowd's reply was patchy and the TV version was tidied up.

claims.text: John Paul II prayed in Warsaw for the Spirit to "renew the face of the earth. Of this land."
claims.note: He said it in Victory Square on 2 June 1979. Many later saw it as the spark for Solidarity.

reigns.hook: Ten million Poles join Solidarity. Moscow is furious, and the man it trusts to restore order is a general in dark glasses.

reigns.tagline: The general who sent in the tanks, then gave in
reigns.reignEnded: Handed over to an elected president
reigns.previously: Strikes win a free union, Solidarity. Gierek falls.
paragraphs: Stanisław Kania ran the party for a year after Gierek. Then the job went to Wojciech Jaruzelski, a stiff general from a gentry family. In 1941 the Soviets had deported his family to Siberia, where his father died. He came back with the Polish army formed in the USSR. He was already defence minister and prime minister. In October 1981 he took the party too.

Early on 13 December 1981 he declared martial law on television. Tanks filled the streets, phones went dead and thousands of Solidarity activists, Wałęsa among them, were interned. At the Wujek mine, police shot nine miners dead. Solidarity was banned. In 1984 secret police officers kidnapped and murdered Father Jerzy Popiełuszko, a priest whose sermons drew huge crowds.

By 1988 the economy was in ruins and strikes were back. In 1989 Jaruzelski's team sat down with Solidarity at the Round Table. In the partly free elections of 4 June, Solidarity won almost every seat it was allowed to contest. Jaruzelski became president by one vote, and Tadeusz Mazowiecki became the first non-communist prime minister in the Soviet bloc. Then he agreed to step down early.

claims.text: He wore dark glasses because Siberian snow damaged his eyes.
claims.note: Jaruzelski said so throughout his life, and biographers accept it: snow-blindness while doing forced labour in the Altai in the early 1940s.

claims.text: Martial law saved Poland from a Soviet invasion.
claims.note: Jaruzelski insisted on it until he died. Soviet Politburo papers released later suggest Moscow had already decided not to send troops.

claims.text: Father Popiełuszko was murdered by officers of the communist secret police.
claims.note: Four officers were tried and convicted at Toruń in 1985. Who gave the order has never been settled.

reigns.hook: Communism is gone, but the general is still president. Poles want to choose their own, and the shipyard electrician wants the job.

reigns.relationToPredecessor: Led the movement that beat him
reigns.cameToPower: Won the first popular presidential vote
reigns.previously: The Round Table ends communism. Jaruzelski agrees to go early.
paragraphs: From here the deck follows the presidents. Lech Wałęsa was an electrician at the Lenin Shipyard in Gdańsk, fired in 1976 for union activity. In August 1980 he joined the strike and soon led it, signing the Gdańsk Agreement with a giant souvenir pen. Under martial law he was interned for nearly a year. In 1983 he won the Nobel Peace Prize, and his wife Danuta collected it in Oslo for him.

He led Solidarity's side at the 1989 Round Table and in 1990 ran for president, beating the outsider Stan Tymiński in the run-off. At his inauguration the last president-in-exile, Ryszard Kaczorowski, handed him the pre-war state insignia. These were the years of "shock therapy", Leszek Balcerowicz's crash switch to a market economy: prices freed, inflation tamed, but many jobs lost.
The last Russian combat troops left in 1993. Wałęsa clashed constantly with parliament and governments. In 1995 he lost a close run-off to the ex-communist Aleksander Kwaśniewski.

claims.text: Wałęsa got into the shipyard to join the strike by climbing over the fence.
claims.note: That is his own account of 14 August 1980, and the jump became the founding image of Solidarity.

claims.text: Danuta Wałęsa collected the Nobel Peace Prize for him.
claims.note: He stayed in Poland in December 1983, fearing he would not be allowed back in. She accepted it with their son Bogdan.

claims.text: The last president-in-exile handed Wałęsa the insignia of the pre-war republic.
claims.note: Ryszard Kaczorowski brought them from London to his swearing-in in December 1990, ending the government-in-exile.

reigns.hook: The man who beats the legend is a smooth, young ex-communist minister who is very good on television.

reigns.tagline: The ex-communist who took Poland into NATO and the EU
reigns.previously: Wałęsa, the Solidarity legend, loses the 1995 vote.
paragraphs: Aleksander Kwaśniewski had been a young sports minister in the last communist governments and sat at the Round Table on the government side. Afterwards he rebuilt the old party into a modern centre-left one. In 1995 he beat Wałęsa by a few points, and many old Solidarity voters were horrified.

He turned out to be a calm, popular president. A new constitution was passed in 1997 and approved in a referendum. In 1999 Poland joined NATO, and on 1 May 2004 it joined the European Union. In 2000 he was re-elected in the first round. He sent Polish troops into the 2003 invasion of Iraq, and in 2004 he helped broker talks in Ukraine's Orange Revolution. After two full terms he had to stand down.

claims.text: Kwaśniewski won re-election in 2000 without needing a run-off.
claims.note: He took about 54 percent in the first round; Wałęsa, trying for a comeback, got about 1 percent.

claims.text: Polish special forces took part in the 2003 invasion of Iraq.
claims.note: GROM commandos fought alongside US and British forces; Poland then led a multinational division in Iraq.

claims.text: The 1997 constitution was approved by referendum.
claims.note: Voters backed it on 25 May 1997, though turnout was only about 43 percent.
