paragraphs: Lech Kaczyński and his identical twin Jarosław were famous at 12, starring in the 1962 children's film "The Two Who Stole the Moon". Lech became a labour lawyer, advised the Gdańsk strikers in 1980 and was interned under martial law. With his brother he founded the Law and Justice party (PiS). As Mayor of Warsaw he opened the Warsaw Rising Museum in 2004.

In 2005 he beat Donald Tusk for the presidency. For a while in 2006 and 2007 his twin was prime minister. Lech was a firm conservative and deeply wary of Russia. In August 2008 he flew to Tbilisi during Russia's war with Georgia and warned that Ukraine, the Baltic states and Poland could be next.

On 10 April 2010 he flew to Russia for a ceremony marking 70 years since the Katyn massacre. His plane crashed while trying to land in thick fog near Smolensk. All 96 people aboard died, including his wife Maria, the army chief of staff and the last president-in-exile. The cause became a bitter political dispute in Poland.

claims.text: The Kaczyński twins starred together in a children's film.
claims.note: They played the two boys in "O dwóch takich, co ukradli księżyc" (1962), based on a book by Kornel Makuszyński.

claims.text: In Tbilisi he warned that after Georgia, Russia could turn on Ukraine, the Baltics and Poland.
claims.note: He said it at a rally in Tbilisi on 12 August 2008, alongside the leaders of Ukraine and the Baltic states.

claims.text: The Polish government's 2011 investigation blamed a descent below safe height in fog.
claims.note: The state accident commission's report also criticised the Russian air traffic controllers. Later inquiries reached different conclusions and remain disputed.

reigns.hook: Under the constitution, the Speaker of the Sejm takes over that same day. His name is Bronisław Komorowski, and an early election must follow.

paragraphs: Bronisław Komorowski was a historian and an old opposition activist, interned under martial law, who had been defence minister and then Speaker of the Sejm. When the president's plane went down on 10 April 2010, the constitution made him acting head of state the same day.

In the early election that summer he ran for Civic Platform, the party of Prime Minister Donald Tusk, and beat the dead president's twin, Jarosław Kaczyński, in the run-off. He was sworn in on 6 August 2010. His were quiet years at the top: steady growth, and Poland co-hosting the Euro 2012 football championship with Ukraine. In 2015 he looked a safe bet for a second term, then lost the run-off to Andrzej Duda.

reigns.tagline: Ten years of court fights and a war next door
reigns.previously: Komorowski, once the clear favourite, loses the 2015 race.
paragraphs: Andrzej Duda was a lawyer from Kraków who had worked in Lech Kaczyński's chancellery and sat briefly in the European Parliament. Running for Law and Justice (PiS), he won the 2015 run-off with 51.55 percent. That autumn PiS won a majority in parliament on its own, and set about remaking the courts and the constitutional tribunal. Brussels accused Poland of undermining the rule of law, and in 2017 it launched the EU's Article 7 procedure.

Duda mostly signed what the government sent him, though in July 2017, after mass street protests, he vetoed two of its court laws. He won a second term in 2020, narrowly beating Rafał Trzaskowski. When Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022, millions of refugees crossed into Poland, and Poles opened their homes to them. In 2023 PiS lost power to Tusk's coalition, and Duda's last years were a running feud with the new government.

claims.text: Duda vetoed two of the government's court reforms in 2017.
claims.note: He announced the vetoes on 24 July 2017 after protests across Poland; he signed revised versions later that year.

claims.text: The EU triggered Article 7 against Poland over the rule of law.
claims.note: The European Commission started the procedure in December 2017, the first time it had ever been used.

claims.text: Duda won the 2020 run-off by about two points.
claims.note: He took 51.03 percent against Trzaskowski's 48.97.

reigns.tagline: The historian and ex-boxer who took on the government
reigns.previously: Duda leaves after ten years and a bruising feud with Tusk.
paragraphs: Karol Nawrocki grew up in Gdańsk, boxed and played football as a young man, and became a historian of the anti-communist resistance. He ran the Museum of the Second World War in Gdańsk from 2017, then the Institute of National Remembrance, which keeps the communist secret police files. PiS picked him in late 2024, though he ran as an independent "citizens' candidate".

He came second in the first round, then beat Warsaw's mayor Rafał Trzaskowski in the run-off on 1 June 2025 with 50.89 percent. He was sworn in on 6 August 2025. He quickly picked fights with Tusk's government, vetoing its bills and sending in his own. He demanded war reparations from Germany, called for a new constitution, and in June 2026 stripped Ukraine's President Zelensky of Poland's highest honour. His story is still being written.

claims.text: Nawrocki won the presidency by under two points.
claims.note: Official results gave him 50.89 percent to Trzaskowski's 49.11 in the run-off of 1 June 2025.

claims.text: He wrote a crime book under a pen name, then praised it as if it were someone else's.
claims.note: He published a book about a communist-era gangster as "Tadeusz Batyr" and admitted it after journalists exposed it during the 2025 campaign.

claims.text: He revoked Zelensky's Order of the White Eagle.
claims.note: He did so on 19 June 2026, angry that a Ukrainian army unit had been named after the wartime UPA, which massacred Poles in Volhynia.
